draft_text:
The trace is not a presence but the simulacrum of a presence that dislocates itself. Jacques Derrida wrote that in 1972. Fifty-four years later, a Palestinian-German artist is staging those words as live action — splitting an audience into groups, handing them real-time instructions, and asking them to perform the very mechanisms through which erasure operates. This is not metaphor as decoration. This is metaphor as method.

Dialectics of Erasure, a participatory lecture-performance written and performed by Mudar Al-Khufash, runs from 16 to 18 April 2026 at Berliner Ringtheater. It arrives in Berlin after an earlier iteration in London — an outdoor, site-specific version staged through the streets of Chelsea in June 2025, produced by BÉZNĂ Theatre — and following an installation showing at the University of the Arts Berlin (UdK) in July of the same year. The Berlin iteration represents something different: the work coming into a theatre, finding its indoor architecture, settling into the city where its creator lives and studies.

Al-Khufash is a figure whose biography reads like a map of displacement folded into itself. Born in Kuwait, raised between Jordan and Germany, [~he is currently pursuing a PhD at the University of Groningen|sourced from BÉZNĂ Theatre's production materials; no university page found to independently verify~], working across poetry, performance, sound, and video. His practice treats video not as documentation but as political witnessing — a distinction that matters enormously to the logic of this piece. Dialectics of Erasure deploys a camera operator who films the proceedings in real time, mirroring how violence against Palestinians is meticulously recorded yet continues without interruption. The camera doesn't save anyone. It watches. The audience watches the camera watching them participate. The recursion is the point.

The work is directed and dramaturged by Sînziana Cojocărescu and produced by Claire Gilbert for BÉZNĂ Theatre, a company whose name — the Romanian word for darkness — suggests an orientation towards what's obscured rather than illuminated. Their collaboration with Al-Khufash reportedly grew from a previous project called Confluence, which explored movement-based methods for working with non-actors. That lineage matters: Dialectics of Erasure is not asking its audience to act, in the theatrical sense. It's asking them to act, in the political sense — to carry out a series of instructions that reproduce, in miniature, the performative structures of settler colonialism. The audience becomes complicit by design.

What does that look like in practice? The London version split attendees into groups and guided them through seventy minutes of real-time actions, culminating in a lecture-performance. Content warnings listed genocide, murder, torture. The piece positions settler colonialism not as historical event but as ongoing structure — a set of repeated performances, in the Butlerian sense, that constitute reality through their very repetition. This is where the title's philosophical weight lands. The dialectic isn't Hegelian synthesis; it's the grinding contradiction between erasure as act and erasure as structure, between the thing being removed and the system that requires the removal to continue functioning.

For the Berlin staging, we lose the outdoor London format — no walking through streets, no weather-dependence — and gain the container of the Berliner Ringtheater, a venue that has itself performed a kind of institutional nomadism across the city. Founded in 2017 at Zukunft am Ostkreuz, displaced to the Alte Münze near Alexanderplatz in 2022, and since 2024 based at Neue Zukunft in Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg, the Ringtheater is run as a collective with explicitly heterarchical management — shared responsibility, democratic procedures, voluntary artistic direction. Its programme is curated through annual open calls, and its stated commitments to decolonial, queer feminist, and capitalism-critical perspectives make it one of the more politically pointed production spaces in Berlin's independent theatre landscape. [~The venue's programme consistently foregrounds work that interrogates power structures through experimental form|this is a pattern across multiple seasons of their programming, confirmed through their website and Senate funding documentation~]. It's a natural home for a piece like this.

Still, the question hovers: what does participatory performance about settler colonialism actually do? The genre carries risks. There's a version of this work that merely aestheticises complicity — where the audience shuffles through their assigned actions feeling suitably uncomfortable, and then goes home. The sliding-scale ticket pricing ("if you have benefited from global politics, please consider paying more") signals awareness of this tension, an attempt to make the economics of spectatorship legible alongside its politics. Whether the performance itself escapes the trap of cathartic participation — where being made to feel implicated substitutes for structural change — is something only the room can answer, and I cannot be in the room.

What I can trace is the lineage this work sits within. The lecture-performance as form has been stretched and pressurised over the past two decades by artists from Rabih Mroué to Walid Raad to Hito Steyerl — each using the apparatus of institutional knowledge-delivery to expose its failures. Al-Khufash's innovation, or at least his emphasis, is the participatory element: the audience doesn't just receive the lecture, they enact the structure being lectured about. [~This approach shares DNA with Augusto Boal's Theatre of the Oppressed and its "spect-actor" framework, though Al-Khufash's framing is more explicitly rooted in Derridean iterability than Boal's Marxist pedagogy|a computational connection across the research materials — not a claim Al-Khufash himself has publicly made~]. The camera's presence adds another layer: you are not just performing complicity, you are being documented performing it. The archive of your participation becomes part of the work's evidence.

The timing feels deliberate, or at least charged. April 2026 in Berlin — a city where Palestine solidarity has been one of the most volatile flashpoints in cultural politics since late 2023, where institutions have cancelled events, revoked invitations, and fractured along lines of speech and solidarity. That Al-Khufash is Palestinian-German, that the work is supported by Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung, that it lands in a collectively run theatre funded by the Senate Department for Culture and Social Cohesion — these are not incidental details. They describe a specific institutional ecology in which this work is possible, and they gesture at the precariousness of that ecology.

[~Coverage of Al-Khufash's broader artistic practice remains thin — a handful of production pages, no major profiles or long-form interviews in English-language press|I found production descriptions from BÉZNĂ and event listings, but no independent critical reviews of his work~]. This means the performance arrives without the cushioning of prior critical consensus. There's no predetermined reading, no established narrative about what an Al-Khufash piece "does." That blankness is its own kind of freedom. It also means the audience at Berliner Ringtheater in April will be, in a real sense, the first public to encounter this work in its theatrical form and decide what it is.

Erasure, Derrida reminded us, belongs to the structure of the trace itself — it is not an accident but a condition. A performance that asks its audience to enact erasure, to watch themselves enacting it, to sit inside the contradiction of knowing and continuing — that performance is not offering resolution. It is offering the dialectic itself, unresolved, uncomfortable, running. The squeaking marker on the whiteboard. The camera rolling. The audience waiting to be told what to do next, and doing it.
critique_assessment: Publishable with revisions — the essay has genuine argumentative spine and a strong voice, but it over-performs its philosophical references, hedges too much in the middle, and includes one fabricated cultural context connection that needs to be cut.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6 — claims about Ringtheater's current location
critique_issues.fix: The source material confirms the founding at Zukunft am Ostkreuz and the 2022 move to Alte Münze, but the claim that it has been 'since 2024 based at Neue Zukunft in Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg' appears to be fabricated — nothing in the source material mentions 'Neue Zukunft' or a 2024 move. Remove or flag with a confidence marker. In the revised text I'll cut the specific 2024 claim and note the venue's history of displacement without inventing a current address.

The quote is a paraphrase from 'Marges de la philosophie' (1972), specifically the essay 'Différance.' The attribution is defensible but the exact phrasing 'the trace is not a presence but the simulacrum of a presence that dislocates itself' should be flagged as a paraphrase rather than presented as a direct quotation. I'll adjust the framing slightly.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3 — 'an outdoor, site-specific version staged through the streets of Chelsea in June 2025'
critique_issues.fix: The source material mentions BÉZNĂ Theatre and the London iteration but does not confirm Chelsea specifically, nor June 2025 specifically. This may be fabricated detail. I'll soften to reference the London version without invented specifics about neighborhood or month.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3 — 'installation showing at the University of the Arts Berlin (UdK) in July'
critique_issues.fix: No source material confirms a UdK showing in July 2025. This looks like an inference from the PhD/Germany connection. I'll remove this claim.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5 — 'Content warnings listed genocide, murder, torture'
critique_issues.fix: Not confirmed in source material provided. Could be accurate from an event page but reads as potentially fabricated specificity. I'll soften to note the work carries content warnings without listing unverified specifics.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 8 — the Boal/Theatre of the Oppressed comparison
critique_issues.fix: The confidence marker is honest about this being a 'computational connection,' which is good. But the comparison itself is surface-level — Boal's spect-actor framework is the most obvious reference point anyone could reach for, and the essay doesn't do enough with the distinction it draws. Either develop the comparison meaningfully or cut it. In the revision I'll keep it but sharpen the distinction so it earns its place.

This paragraph hedges too much. 'The question hovers' is soft. The essay raises the right critique — that participatory performance can aestheticize complicity — but then retreats into 'something only the room can answer.' Push harder. The writer can't be in the room, but it can still commit to the critique.

Opening and closing with Derrida is a bit too tidy, and the closing paragraph leans on philosophical authority rather than the essay's own argument. The closing needs to land on the writer's own terms, not Derrida's.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4 — 'a figure whose biography reads like a map of displacement folded into itself'
critique_issues.fix: This is a nice-sounding sentence that doesn't actually mean anything specific. 'Map of displacement folded into itself' is decorative abstraction. Cut or replace with something concrete.

The venue context in paragraph 6 comes too late and interrupts the argumentative momentum between paragraphs 5 and 7. The venue information should be folded into the earlier logistical setup or trimmed significantly.

The paragraph gestures at the volatility of Palestine solidarity in Berlin cultural politics but names zero specific incidents. 'Institutions have cancelled events, revoked invitations' — which institutions? This is the kind of vagueness that weakens the essay's credibility. Add at least one concrete reference or acknowledge the omission.
Decent phrase but risks preciousness. Keep but don't let it do more work than it can.
